newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan warms to idea of investing in hedge funds.
newsitem.headline: Japan warms to idea of investing in hedge funds.

text.p: Japanese financial institutions, reknowned for their timidity, are now aiming to take their place alongside big market players through the country's first hedge fund.

Nomura International Plc, a wholly owned subsidiary of Nomura Securities Co Ltd, Japan's largest broker, recently launched a special fund, the Epic Fund, whose investment strategy is similar to that of U.S. hedge funds, bank sources here said.
Nomura International appears to have collected up to $2.0 billion from investors in Japan and other countries, they said.

In another signal of a greater boldness in the use of hedge funds than previously seen in the Japanese financial industry, some officials at major Japanese banks also said they were considering entrusting money directly to U.S. hedge funds.

Nomura's Epic Fund is going for high returns through investment in such vehicles as currencies, securities and commodities in combination with futures, repurchase agreements and derivatives, they said.
Nomura Securities Co Ltd here said it was not involved in the deal and a spokeswoman at Nomura International in London declined to comment.
"We are prevented from making any comment about the Epic fund...other than to acknowledge that it does exist," she said.

An official at a major Japanese bank in Tokyo said the bank was investing in the fund because it was innovative and a product that Japanese brokers have not offered, describing it as "a Japanese version of a hedge fund".

Nomura International is in charge of sales of funds, while a Hong Kong-based Nomura unit is responsible for investment advice. The fund is an open-end type of mutual fund in which investors can withdraw funds after a year, or add assets.

The fund is basically adopting a so-called "Marco" strategy in which fund managers take positions in advance -- either buy or sell -- by predicting certain market movements in the future and then reverse them to take profits when they actually occur in line with their expectations.
This is a strategy commonly used among U.S. hedge funds, including one headed by a financier George Soros.
Hedge funds are highly leveraged and aggressively managed by investment funds and often exempt from disclosure.

"We are just examining how the (Epic) fund will perform and are also hoping to learn their expertise," said the Japanese bank official. "It is also necessary to let internal traders compete with the external funds over performance," he added.
Commenting on the developments, a Japanese Finance Ministry official said the ministry welcomes trends leading to an increase of cross-border investments by Japanese investors.

Over the past five years, Japanese financial institutions had been wary of taking investment risks, particularly in cross-border transactions, in the aftermath of the collapse in the early 1990s of the asset inflated "bubble economy".
At the same time, U.S. financial institutions and hedge funds have grown in prominence in the market.
But a prolonged period of low interest rates and sluggish lending business at home have made Japanese financial institutions more intrepid about putting money in hedge funds.
"Now it's time to catch up with them (other players) gradually by exploring new skills and know-how," said the bank official.

Bankers said this move could eventually prove a breakthrough to cross-border investment by Japanese investors, although they are not yet confident enough to allocate a large sum of money to the hedge funds.
